claims.text: Conventional preparation of single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 typically has notable residual porosity.
Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 typically contains microstructural defects.
Residual porosity in ZrB2 is associated with structural degradation during exposure to aggressive liquid plating environments.
Spark plasma sintering can densify single-phase ZrB2 below 2300 °C.
SPS at approximately 1800 °C with applied uniaxial pressure is proposed as the lower-temperature preparation route.
Rapid heating and applied pressure in SPS accelerate mass transport and densification in ZrB2.
Rapid pressure-assisted sintering minimizes grain growth in ZrB2.
Rapid pressure-assisted sintering minimizes pore coalescence in ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have fewer and smaller residual pores than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
A denser ZrB2 microstructure is less susceptible to infiltration by a liquid plating bath.
Reduced liquid infiltration will reduce hole formation in ZrB2 during prolonged plating-bath exposure.
Reduced hole formation will mitigate eventual component failure.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have greater mechanical strength and integrity than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will resist plating-induced damage better than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
The lower-temperature SPS treatment must preserve single-phase ZrB2.
Performance is to be assessed under extended immersion in a representative liquid plating bath at its operational temperature.
A controlled comparison will use conventionally sintered specimens and SPS specimens exposed for approximately 200 hours under standardized bath conditions.
Porosity, density, grain size, phase, mechanical properties, and post-exposure holes or defects will be measured.

The hypothesis is falsified if SPS produces no statistically significant porosity or mechanical-property improvement and no measurable reduction in plating-induced defects relative to the conventional control.
